results.evidence: TLDR cites 'CA Vehicle Code § 13558, FL Statute § 322.2615, TX Transportation Code § 724.041' — three specific statute numbers that violate the no-statute-citation rule for blog content
Names 'Lawrence Taylor, author of Drunk Driving Defense' and 'F. Lee Bailey, author of Excellence in Cross-Examination' as individual legal experts — both prohibited under the no-named-attorney rule

State-specific suspension lengths ('California: 4-month suspension... 1-year for refusal', 'Florida: 6 months or 12 months', 'Texas: 90-day... 180-day') are stated as factual claims with no parenthetical source citation

All procedural claims are jurisdiction-qualified — 'most states give you a narrow window', explicit state names (California, Florida, Texas, New York), and 'In most states, you get a temporary permit'
no issues found
License suspension consequences are tied to explicit state jurisdictions (California, Florida, Texas, New York) rather than stated as universal facts

results.reason: No question_count field in frontmatter to validate against; body contains multiple reader-to-attorney questions as designed.
Statutes cited (CA Vehicle Code § 13558, FL § 322.2615, TX Transportation Code § 724.041), Lawrence Taylor and F. Lee Bailey named with book titles, NHTSA referenced for FST protocols.
Action items use plain language ('call your attorney', 'write that date on your phone', 'file it yourself'); legal terms like ALR and FST appear with context.
None of the banned phrases ('end of the day', 'tip of iceberg', 'slippery slope', 'double-edged sword', 'game changer', 'wake-up call') appear.
Consistent second person 'you/your' throughout; brief third-person references to 'the officer' and 'defendants' are subjects of discussion, not voice shifts.
Active voice dominates; passive constructions ('was arrested', 'is preserved') appear occasionally but well below 30%.
'Arraignment', 'preponderance', and 'retainer' appear without explicit definition on first use, though context helps.
Logical flow: hook -> two-system problem -> miss-deadline consequences -> why it matters -> three actions -> question list -> big picture -> CTA.
Multiple clear CTAs: five attorney questions, DUI Defense Playbook ($97), Case Decoder ($197), free Case Progress Score, and file-it-yourself instructions.
Action statements are direct imperatives ('call', 'write', 'file', 'ask', 'bookmark'); hedges like 'may' appear only on informational claims.
No paragraph exceeds 300 words; action-oriented paragraphs stay under 100 words.
Word count is distributed across 7+ sections; the 'Three Things' section is longest but below 50% of total.
Every threat (automatic suspension, missed deadline, lost discovery) is paired with a specific action within 2 sentences (file the form, set a reminder, ask the attorney).
Strong hook ('Your license is about to disappear'), evidence-rich middle with state-by-state data and expert citations, empowering close with five questions and file-it-yourself instruction.

results.evidence: Contains direct commands like 'call your attorney right now', 'Write that date on your phone's calendar', 'file it yourself', and 'Set a recurring daily alarm on your phone' — phrased as instructions to follow without attorney guidance.

Sections like 'What Happens If You Miss the Deadline' instruct the reader to 'file it yourself' without a proximate redirect to consult an attorney about whether self-filing is appropriate for their situation.
Post discusses DMV hearings generally and asks reader to pose questions to their attorney; does not render judgment like 'your case is strong' about the reader's specific circumstances.
Recommends the reader take a specific procedural step: 'If your attorney hasn't filed by day 7, file it yourself' and 'you can file it yourself' regarding the DMV administrative hearing request.
Post does not discuss immigration consequences, deportation, visa status, DACA, or green card issues, so immigration redirect is not applicable.
Suspension periods and deadlines are sourced to 'CA Vehicle Code § 13558, FL Statute § 322.2615, TX Transportation Code § 724.041' in the TLDRBox.
Only names Lawrence Taylor and F. Lee Bailey as authors of legal texts, not as recommended service providers; no bail bond companies or law firms are named with a recommendation.
Post does not use 'we recommend,' 'we advise,' or 'we suggest' in legal-action contexts; 'we' only appears in 'read our walkthrough' and 'What We Do' product section.

Multiple unlabeled scenarios appear as vivid second-person narratives: 'You walk out of the police station at 4 AM...', 'You stare at the calendar and realize it's day 11', and 'The hearing officer calls your case number' — none marked as hypothetical.

Frames self-action as empowering without attorney: 'you can file it yourself — and that five-minute action may be the most important thing you do for your defense' implies the reader can handle the DMV filing independently.
Uses qualifiers like 'most states give you roughly 10 days,' 'The specifics vary by state,' and 'in most states, you get a temporary permit' when discussing legal rules.
Outcome language is hedged: 'testimony that could win your criminal trial,' 'may be the most important thing you do,' and state-by-state variation is explicitly noted in the disclaimer.
Strategies are attributed to Lawrence Taylor ('Drunk Driving Defense') and F. Lee Bailey ('Excellence in Cross-Examination'), with statutes cited; not presented as the blog's original legal opinions.

State deadline variations (CA 10 days, FL 10 days, TX 15 days, NY no separate hearing) are presented as jurisdictional differences, not contradictions; post consistently frames DMV and criminal as separate proceedings.

DUI Defense Playbook is framed as '26 questions for your attorney' and 'cheat sheet for your next attorney meeting'; Case Decoder 'generates 15 questions calibrated to your specific case' — both positioned as attorney-prep research tools.

Opens with 'Your license is about to disappear and nobody told you' naming the fear; H2s like 'What Happens If You Miss the Deadline' and 'Three Things Your Attorney Should Do With the DMV Hearing' are action/outcome-oriented.
Legal terms are defined inline (e.g., 'preponderance vs. beyond reasonable doubt', 'free deposition', 'ALR hearing' shown with state context); paragraphs stay under 4 sentences throughout.

A concrete action ('call your attorney right now and ask: Have you filed the DMV administrative hearing request?') appears in the TLDRBox before the first H2, but it isn't formatted as a distinct immediate-action block separate from the summary.
Every decision point leads with a default — e.g., 'File the Request on Day One' and 'If your attorney hasn't filed by day 7, file it yourself' provide clear leading recommendations.
'The questions to ask your DUI attorney this week' section lists 5 unranked items without a 'start with these' priority marker.
system-decoder-post — decodes the two-track DUI system (criminal vs DMV) and explains the strategic mechanics of the DMV hearing.
Every suspension stat (CA 4-month, FL 6-month, TX 90-day) is followed within 2 sentences by an action like 'Search your state's DMV website right now for administrative hearing request form'.
No blame language — the post consistently frames the attorney or the system as the failure point, never the defendant ('nobody told you', 'your attorney was busy').

Opens validating fear ('Your license is about to disappear'), middle decodes the two-system mechanics, and closes on agency ('Set a recurring daily alarm... Do not turn it off until you have written confirmation').
Only H2/H3 heading levels used, key actions are bolded, no tables, and H2 sections stay within roughly 300-500 words each.

Every H2 section contains one standalone bolded sentence under 27 words — e.g., 'The DMV hearing is the only time in the entire DUI process where the officer testifies under oath with no prosecutor guiding the questions.'

All three FAQ answers start with the direct answer, stay 3-4 sentences, and read naturally as peer replies ('Your license gets automatically suspended...', 'The DMV hearing forces the arresting officer to testify under oath...').
